title: One person, two natures
hookLine: Chalcedon: without confusion, change, division or separation

cards: A boat in a storm on the Sea of Galilee. Waves coming over the side. The disciples bailing, shouting.
And in the back of the boat, Mark's Gospel says, Jesus is "asleep on a pillow." Worn out, like any man after a long day. They shake him awake.
Then "he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still." And the sea goes flat. A tired man asleep on a cushion, then a voice the wind obeys.
Same boat, same person. How do you say who that is, without dropping one half? Today's word: one person.

teach.b: The Gospels keep doing this. On the way to the tomb of his friend Lazarus, John's Gospel has two words: "Jesus wept." A few lines later the same Jesus stands at the grave and cries, "Lazarus, come forth."
Grief, and then a voice that calls the dead. Christians searched for words that keep both.

At the council of Chalcedon, bishops said Christ is one person in two natures, truly God and truly human. And they added four guard rails, each a without. Without confusion: the two aren't blended into some third thing.
Without change: neither turns into the other. Without division, and without separation: there aren't two people in the boat, one sleeping and one commanding. It's one who.
One of the council's Greek words for person was hypostasis: the who, the one acting in everything he does.
So the same one weeps and calls Lazarus out; the same one sleeps and stills the sea. Not a man who was only very holy. Not God wearing a human costume.
Both, not either. Not every church accepted Chalcedon's exact wording; some ancient churches of the east prefer to speak of one united nature, and they too confess him fully God and fully human.
Day seven hundred eighty-three told that story. Today the point is the shape of the answer. It doesn't solve the mystery.
It refuses to drop either half of it.

how: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that hold the early creeds accept Chalcedon's definition of Christ as one person in two natures, while the Oriental Orthodox churches speak of one united nature; all of them confess him truly God and truly human.

o: Christ as one who, truly God and truly human
God the Father and Jesus as the same person
Jesus as a man so holy he later became divine

s: Chalcedon said there were two people in the boat, one sleeping and one commanding
without division and without separation: one person, the same one who sleeps and stills the sea.
on the way to Lazarus's tomb, Jesus wept, and then called the dead man out
"Jesus wept." a few lines later: "Lazarus, come forth."
Chalcedon blended God and human into a new third thing
without confusion and without change: neither nature turns into the other.

games.q: you're in the boat. Jesus is asleep on a pillow while the storm rises. you wake him. what happens?
o: he rebukes the wind: peace, be still, and the sea goes calm.
he tells everyone to swim for shore.
games.why: he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still. a tired man and a voice the wind obeys: one person.

practice: Rest one hand, palm up, on each knee: in the left, something true about your life that's hard; in the right, something true that's good.
Don't let either cancel the other, or rush to decide which is really true; feel the two weights, and one breath going in and out between them.
If you pray, hold the line from Mark, Peace, be still; if you don't, just keep both hands open.

wordCard.voice: One person. Chalcedon's answer: Christ is one person, truly God and truly human, two natures without confusion, change, division or separation.
